summary.text:
Writing \(n=qt\) for an odd prime divisor \(q\), an LTE/Legendre valuation count on the factors \(2^{(q-1)j}-1\) shows \(q\mid a(qt-1)\) whenever \(t\ge2\), contradicting the hypothesis since \(q
mid2^{qt-2}\); powers \(n=2^e\) are excluded by \(v_2((2^e-1)!)=2^e-1-e\), which gives \(v_2(a(2^e-1))=e-1\). For the resulting prime \(p\), the hypothesis gives \(p
mid a(p-1)\), while any order \(r<p-1\) of 2 modulo \(p\) would make the numerator factor \(2^r-1\) divisible by \(p\), and since \(p
mid(p-1)!\) this would force \(p\mid a(p-1)\); hence the order is \(p-1\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P_m=\prod_{1\le k<m}(2^k-1),\qquad
N_m=2^{m-1}P_m
\]
for every positive integer \(m\). Thus the sequence in the question is
\[
a(m)=\frac{N_m}{m!}
 =\frac{2^{m-1}}{m!}\prod_{k=1}^{m-1}(2^k-1).
\]
We will first establish that this quotient is an integer and develop the divisibility estimates needed later.

For a prime \(q\) and a positive integer \(x\), write \(v_q(x)\) for the exponent of \(q\) in \(x\).

### 1. A valuation estimate for the factors \(2^k-1\)

We need the following elementary consequence of Fermat's theorem.

**Lemma 1.** If \(q\) is an odd prime and \(j\ge 1\), then
\[
q^{v_q(j)+1}\mid 2^{(q-1)j}-1.
\]

Indeed, Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
q\mid 2^{q-1}-1.
\]
Put \(X=2^{q-1}\), and write \(j=q^s u\), where \(s=v_q(j)\) and \(q\nmid u\). Starting with \(q\mid X-1\), one obtains inductively
\[
q^{r+1}\mid X^{q^r}-1\qquad(r\ge0).
\]
To see the induction step, factor
\[
Y^q-1=(Y-1)(1+Y+\cdots+Y^{q-1}).
\]
If \(q\mid Y-1\), then \(Y\equiv1\pmod q\), so the second factor is congruent to \(q\), hence is divisible by \(q\). Thus passing from \(Y-1\) to \(Y^q-1\) gains at least one additional factor of \(q\). Applying this with \(Y=X^{q^r}\) proves the displayed induction. In particular,
\[
q^{s+1}\mid X^{q^s}-1.
\]
Finally, \(X^{q^s}-1\) divides \((X^{q^s})^u-1=X^j-1\). This proves Lemma 1.

Multiplying Lemma 1 over \(j=1,\dots,t\) gives the useful estimate
\[
q^{\,t+v_q(t!)}
 \mid \prod_{j=1}^t\left(2^{(q-1)j}-1\right).
\tag{1}
\]
This follows because
\[
\sum_{j=1}^t\bigl(v_q(j)+1\bigr)=v_q(t!)+t.
\]

If \((q-1)t<m\), all the indices
\[
(q-1),2(q-1),\dots,t(q-1)
\]
are distinct members of \(\{1,2,\dots,m-1\}\). Consequently their corresponding factors form a subproduct of \(P_m\), and (1) yields
\[
q^{\,t+v_q(t!)}\mid P_m.
\tag{2}
\]

We also recall the standard factorial-valuation identity
\[
v_q((qu+r)!)=u+v_q(u!)\qquad(0\le r<q).
\tag{3}
\]
One way to see this is to use Legendre's formula:
\[
v_q(M!)=\sum_{i\ge1}\left\lfloor\frac{M}{q^i}\right\rfloor.
\]
For \(M=qu+r\), with \(0\le r<q\), the first term is \(u\), while the remaining terms sum to \(v_q(u!)\). We will also use the immediate monotonicity
\[
u\le t\quad\Longrightarrow\quad v_q(u!)\le v_q(t!),
\tag{4}
\]
since \(u!\mid t!\).

### 2. Integrality of the defining quotient

We now prove
\[
m!\mid N_m\qquad(m\ge1).
\tag{5}
\]
It is enough to compare the valuations at every prime \(p\).

For \(p=2\), every number \(2^k-1\) is odd, so
\[
v_2(N_m)=m-1.
\]
On the other hand, \(v_2(m!)\le m-1\) for \(m\ge1\). For example, this follows immediately from Legendre's formula (equivalently, from \(v_2(m!)=m-s_2(m)\), where \(s_2(m)\ge1\) is the sum of the binary digits of \(m\)). Thus the required inequality holds at \(2\).

Now let \(p\) be an odd prime. Set
\[
u=\left\lfloor\frac m p\right\rfloor,
\qquad
T=\left\lfloor\frac{m-1}{p-1}\right\rfloor.
\]
We claim that \(u\le T\). If \(u=0\), this is clear. If \(u\ge1\), then \(up\le m\), and hence
\[
u(p-1)=up-u\le m-1.
\]
Therefore \(u\le\lfloor(m-1)/(p-1)\rfloor=T\).

Writing \(m=pu+r\), where \(0\le r<p\), identity (3) gives
\[
v_p(m!)=u+v_p(u!).
\tag{6}
\]
By the definition of \(T\),
\[
(p-1)T\le m-1<m,
\]
so (2), applied with \(q=p\) and \(t=T\), gives
\[
v_p(P_m)\ge T+v_p(T!).
\]
Using \(u\le T\) and (4), we get
\[
v_p(P_m)\ge T+v_p(T!)
             \ge u+v_p(u!)
             =v_p(m!).
\]
Since the extra factor \(2^{m-1}\) in \(N_m\) is harmless for odd \(p\), this proves \(v_p(N_m)\ge v_p(m!)\). Thus (5) holds for every prime, proving the integrality of \(a(m)=N_m/m!\). In particular,
\[
N_m=a(m)m!.
\tag{7}
\]

### 3. An odd prime divisor of a composite \(n\) also divides \(a(n-1)\)

The next key fact is the following.

**Lemma 2.** Let \(q\) be an odd prime and let \(t\ge2\). Then
\[
q\mid a(qt-1).
\]

Put \(m=qt-1\). Since \(t\ge2\),
\[
(q-1)t=qt-t<qt-1=m.
\]
Thus (2) gives
\[
v_q(P_m)\ge t+v_q(t!).
\tag{8}
\]
On the other hand,
\[
m=qt-1=q(t-1)+(q-1),
\]
where \(0\le q-1<q\). Applying (3) yields
\[
v_q(m!)=(t-1)+v_q((t-1)!).
\tag{9}
\]
Since \((t-1)!\mid t!\), comparison of (8) and (9) gives
\[
v_q(P_m)\ge v_q(m!)+1.
\]
The factor \(2^{m-1}\) is not divisible by the odd prime \(q\), so the same inequality holds for \(N_m\):
\[
v_q(N_m)\ge v_q(m!)+1.
\]
Using \(N_m=a(m)m!\) from (7), we conclude that \(v_q(a(m))\ge1\), proving Lemma 2.

### 4. Powers of two cannot satisfy the hypothesis

We next establish the exact \(2\)-adic identity
\[
v_2((2^e-1)!)+e=2^e-1
\qquad(e\ge0).
\tag{10}
\]
This can be proved by induction. It is immediate for \(e=0\). For the induction step, observe that
\[
2^{e+1}-1=2(2^e-1)+1.
\]
Applying (3) with \(q=2\), \(u=2^e-1\), and \(r=1\), gives
\[
v_2((2^{e+1}-1)!)=(2^e-1)+v_2((2^e-1)!),
\]
and (10) follows from the induction hypothesis.

Suppose now that \(e\ge2\), put
\[
n=2^e,\qquad m=n-1=2^e-1,
\]
and assume, for contradiction, that
\[
2^e\mid a(m)+2^{2^e-2}.
\tag{11}
\]
For \(e\ge2\), one has \(e\le2^e-2\), so
\[
2^e\mid 2^{2^e-2}.
\]
Subtracting this term from (11), we obtain
\[
2^e\mid a(m).
\tag{12}
\]
Because \(N_m=a(m)m!\), (12) would imply
\[
v_2(N_m)\ge e+v_2(m!).
\tag{13}
\]
But every factor in \(P_m\) is odd, so
\[
v_2(N_m)=m-1=2^e-2.
\tag{14}
\]
Meanwhile, (10) says
\[
e+v_2(m!)=2^e-1=m.
\tag{15}
\]
Equations (13)--(15) would give \(2^e-2\ge2^e-1\), a contradiction. Therefore no power \(2^e\) with \(e\ge2\) satisfies the divisibility hypothesis.

### 5. The hypothesis forces \(n\) to be prime

Let \(n>2\) and suppose
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\tag{16}
\]
Every positive integer is either a power of \(2\), or has an odd prime divisor: this follows by removing the largest power of \(2\) from its prime factorization and, if the remaining factor exceeds \(1\), choosing a prime divisor of that odd factor.

If \(n\) is a power of \(2\), then \(n=2^e\). Since \(n>2\), necessarily \(e\ge2\), contradicting the result of the preceding section.

Thus \(n\) has an odd prime divisor \(q\). Write
\[
n=qt.
\]
If \(t=1\), then \(n=q\) is prime, as desired. The possibility \(t=0\) is excluded by \(n>2\). It remains to rule out \(t\ge2\).

If \(t\ge2\), Lemma 2 gives
\[
q\mid a(qt-1)=a(n-1).
\tag{17}
\]
Since \(q\mid n\), hypothesis (16) also gives
\[
q\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}.
\]
Subtracting (17), we find
\[
q\mid2^{n-2}.
\]
Because \(q\) is prime, this implies \(q\mid2\), and hence \(q=2\), contradicting that \(q\) is odd. Therefore \(t\ge2\) is impossible, and \(t=1\). Consequently \(n=q\) is prime.

### 6. In the prime case, \(2\) is a primitive root

It remains to prove the primitive-root conclusion. Let \(p>2\) be prime and suppose
\[
p\mid a(p-1)+2^{p-2}.
\tag{18}
\]
First,
\[
p\nmid a(p-1).
\tag{19}
\]
Indeed, if \(p\mid a(p-1)\), then (18) would imply \(p\mid2^{p-2}\). Since \(p\) is prime, this would imply \(p\mid2\), impossible because \(p>2\).

We claim next that
\[
p\nmid P_{p-1}
 =\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1).
\tag{20}
\]
Suppose otherwise. Then \(p\mid N_{p-1}\), since \(P_{p-1}\) is a factor of \(N_{p-1}\). By (7),
\[
N_{p-1}=a(p-1)(p-1)!.
\]
Euclid's lemma would then imply that \(p\mid a(p-1)\) or \(p\mid(p-1)!\). The first alternative contradicts (19), and the second is impossible because none of the integers \(1,2,\dots,p-1\) is divisible by the prime \(p\). This proves (20).

Now consider the residue class of \(2\) modulo \(p\). It is nonzero, and Fermat's little theorem gives
\[
2^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{21}
\]
We show that no smaller positive exponent gives \(1\). More generally, suppose \(\ell\ge0\) satisfies
\[
2^\ell\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{22}
\]
Divide \(\ell\) by \(p-1\):
\[
\ell=(p-1)s+r,
\qquad 0\le r<p-1.
\]
Using (21) in (22), we obtain
\[
2^r\equiv1\pmod p.
\tag{23}
\]
If \(r>0\), then \(1\le r\le p-2\), and (23) says
\[
p\mid 2^r-1.
\]
But \(2^r-1\) is one of the factors of \(P_{p-1}=\prod_{k=1}^{p-2}(2^k-1)\), so this would imply \(p\mid P_{p-1}\), contrary to (20). Hence \(r=0\), and therefore
\[
p-1\mid\ell.
\]
Thus the multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) is exactly \(p-1\). Since Euler's totient satisfies \(\varphi(p)=p-1\) for prime \(p\), this says precisely that \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(p\).

Applying this final argument to the prime \(n\) obtained in Section 5 proves both conclusions: every \(n>2\) satisfying
\[
n\mid a(n-1)+2^{n-2}
\]
is prime, and \(2\) is a primitive root modulo \(n\).
